phonemes.desc: Rough breathing on upsilon with acute [hýp], the pitch peak of the name.

pronunciation.approximation: 'HOOP-nohs' — the first syllable is pitched high and begins with a rough 'h'; the second is short and level.

kin.label: PIE
kin.form: *sup-nó- 'sleep' (Beekes): Sanskrit svápnaḥ 'sleep, dream', Latin somnus and sopor — a root-family older than Greece; English 'sleep' belongs to a different root.

kin.label: Twin
kin.form: Θάνατος (Thánatos), his twin brother, the personification of death

pronunciation.note: Hýpnos is Tier 2 because the Greek Ὕπνος preserves the acute stress on the first syllable but has no long vowel. He and his twin Thánatos are children of Night (Nyx) and live near the sunset.

domains.title: The Tender-Eyed God
domains.subtitle: Sleep, Dreams, Release
domains.lead: Hýpnos is the personification of sleep, the gentle twin of death who brings rest to gods and mortals. He moves through the world on silent wings, touching tired eyelids with a branch or a whisper.

cards.name: Personified Sleep
cards.desc: One of the children of Nyx; sleep comes to all equally, slave and king.

cards.name: Wings of Quiet
cards.desc: Often shown with wings at his temples or heels, swift and soundless.

cards.name: Dream-Giver
cards.desc: He opens the gates through which the Oneiroi, dream-spirits, pass to sleeping mortals.

cards.name: Brother of Death
cards.desc: Thanatos and Hypnos together carry the dead from the battlefield.

symbols.name: Poppy
symbols.meaning: The soporific flower associated with sleep and dreams

symbols.name: Wings at the temples
symbols.meaning: The swift arrival of sleep and its power to lift the soul into dream

symbols.name: Branch or horn
symbols.meaning: The wand with which he sprinkles sleep upon the eyes

symbols.name: Dark mist
symbols.meaning: The shadowy garment in which he wraps the sleeper

symbols.name: The gates of horn and ivory
symbols.meaning: The two dream-gates of Odyssey 19.562–567: true dreams pass through polished horn, deceitful ones through ivory — Sleep's workshop has two doors, and mortals cannot tell which one was used.

mythology.lead: Hýpnos is a minor but indispensable power. Gods call on him when they need a mortal or immortal to fall unconscious, and poets love him as the brother who daily rescues humanity from wakefulness — and nightly rehearses its death.

myths.title: Hera Bribes the Brother of Death
myths.text: In Iliad 14, Hera needs Zeus unconscious, and she knows where to shop. She finds Hypnos on Lemnos and begs his help; the god refuses, remembering the last time — when he lulled Zeus to aid Heracles, the king of gods hunted him and would have hurled him from heaven into the sea, had not Nyx, swift Night, taken him in: even Zeus shrinks from offending Night (Iliad 14.249–261). Hera offers what a personification of desire cannot refuse — Pasithea, one of the younger Graces, as his bride — and swears it by Styx (14.267–276). Hypnos accepts, pours sleep over Zeus's eyes as the golden cloud closes around the embracing pair on Ida, and Poseidon rallies the Greeks unchecked. The episode is the Iliad's one glimpse of Olympus's backstairs: heaven itself, the poem admits, runs on bribes, grudges, and the judicious administration of oblivion.

myths.title: The Twins Carry Sarpedon Home
myths.text: When Patroklos kills Zeus's son Sarpedon, the father cannot save him — fate forbids — so Zeus does the next thing: he tells Apollo to wash the gore from the body, anoint it, and clothe it in immortal raiment, then hand it over. And there come the gentlest hands in Homer: Hypnos and Thanatos, Sleep and Death, 'swift as thought', bear the hero away to Lycia, land of the broad barley-fields, to his brothers and kinsmen for tomb and stele (Iliad 16.454, 666–683). The scene caught the painters for a thousand years: the krater of Euphronios (c. 515 BCE) shows the twins lifting the limp hero, one at his head, one at his heels, their wings folded with practiced care. Homer gives death its tenderest image by splitting it in two — Thanatos takes the body, but Hypnos takes the pain: the sleep in which nothing hurts is the twin that walks ahead.

myths.title: The House Without Sun
myths.text: Hesiod lodges Hypnos in the family of Night and a geography of gloom. In the Theogony (211–225) he is one of the children Nyx bears without a father — alongside Thanatos, the Keres, Dreams, Blame, and Woe — and near the poem's end (758–761) the poet gives him a house: there have their dwellings Sleep and Death, dread gods; never does the shining sun look upon them with his beams, neither rising nor setting. Homer had already planted the same sunset geography in the Odyssey: at the world's edge lie the land and people of the Cimmerians, wrapped in cloud and mist, on whom the sun never looks (Odyssey 11.14–19). Sleep lives at the far edge of the map because every night the whole human world travels there. The cave of Hypnos is where the sun goes when it leaves us — and the daily rehearsal of that journey is why mortals greet his brother without surprise.

myths.title: The Palace of Somnus and Alcyone's Dream
myths.text: Ovid gives the Roman god his full establishment. When Ceyx drowns at sea, his wife Alcyone prays at Juno's altar, and Iris is dispatched through the gloom to the land of the Cimmerians, to a palace high in the mountains where Somnus lies sunk on an ebony couch in a silence so deep that not even a river stirs (Metamorphoses 11.410–748). Iris rouses him with difficulty; he summons from his thousand dream-sons Morpheus, 'the shaper', who can take any face, and Morpheus appears to Alcyone as her drowned husband and tells her the truth. She finds the true body on the shore, and the gods change both into halcyon kingfishers — whose calm midwinter days, the 'halcyon days', still bless the storm-locked sea in our language. Ovid's Somnus runs a bureau of tailored apparitions: every sleeper is a correspondent, and every dream a message shaped to be believed.

lore.syncretism: The Romans identified Hypnos with Somnus, whose mythology largely mirrors the Greek; Ovid keeps the Cimmerian geography and adds the dream-shaper Morpheus and the palace full of his sons. In later antiquity the winged, poppy-bearing image of Sleep merged with that of Death in funerary art, and Christian writers, while formally demonizing the pagan sleep-gods, retained the poppy, the wings, and the bedchamber vigil in their own depictions of the dying. Modern psychology has reclaimed Hypnos through the term 'hypnosis' — coined by James Braid in the 1840s from the god's name — though the connection is more romantic than clinical.
lore.culturalLegacy: Hýpnos lives wherever humanity manages its own oblivion: in the word hypnosis (Braid's coinage of the 1840s, from the god's name), in morphine, which borrows his son Morpheus' name, and in the whole modern industry of sleep — mattresses, apps, pills, lullabies. He is the god of the third of life we spend unconscious, the realm where memory, fear, and desire recombine. In art he remains a beautiful winged youth, sleep's beauty made visible; his twinship with Thanatos, carved on a thousand sarcophagi, still reminds every viewer that each night's surrender of consciousness is a small rehearsal for the last one.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Hýpnos is the god who visits everyone. Rich and poor, hero and coward, all close their eyes at his touch. In this he is more democratic than any Olympian. Yet he is also dangerous: sleep can be bribery, escape, or the doorway to deception, as when Hera uses him against Zeus.

The Greeks did not trust sleep entirely. Dreams could be true or false, divine or merely digestive — Homer gives them two gates, of horn and of ivory, and no way to know which one a dream came through. Hypnos therefore carries ambivalence: he restores and he disables, he heals and he makes vulnerable. To honor him is to acknowledge our daily surrender of consciousness — the small death without which no waking is possible.
lore.archaeology: Hypnos was represented in Greek and Roman art as a winged youth, often at the bedside of the dying or carrying a hero's body. The most famous single image is ceramic: the krater of Euphronios (c. 515 BCE, Metropolitan Museum, New York) shows Hypnos and Thanatos gently lifting Sarpedon's body, one twin at the head, one at the heels — the Iliad scene rendered by a master of red-figure. In bronze, the head of Hypnos in the British Museum (Roman copy of a Hellenistic type, said to be from Civitella d'Arna) shows the god with wings at his temples. Funerary art across the Roman world pairs the twins on sarcophagi as escorts of the dead — sleep and death made brothers in marble, the gentlest company the departed ever keep.
